newsitem.title: USA: Clinton administration details Washington aid plan.
newsitem.headline: Clinton administration details Washington aid plan.

text.p: The White House on Tuesday announced a $3.9 billion five-year federal aid plan for Washington D.C., and said it was ending the $3.56 billion federal payment to the city it would have made over that period.

Under the plan, the White House said in a statement, the Federal goverment would assume the city's pension liabilities for police, firefighters, judges and teachers. Overall, the net cost of the plan to the federal government comes to $339 million over five years, it said.
The $3.9 billion includes $2.46 billion to operate the city's court and prison system as well as to fund prison renovation and construction.

The total also includes $917 million to boost the federal share of the city's Medicaid payments, $125 million to help rebuild Washington's transportation infrastructure and $117 million to improve the city's tax collection.
The White House statement also said that the plan would provide unspecified grants and tax incentives for economic development in the city.
The plan is expected to be contained in President Bill Clinton's fiscal 1998 budget proposal, due to be sent to Congress on Feb. 6.

Clinton's plan would end the annual $660 million payment that the U.S. makes to the District for the federal government's use of city property, saving another $3.56 billion over five years, the White House said.

Also, the federal government would assume responsibility for existing pension plans for police, firefighters and others. These plans would close once they are transferred to the federal government, which means no new liability would incur, the White House said.
"The existing pension assets would pay the beneficiaries," the White House said.

And, starting in 2007, the federal government would pay off, over an extended period of time, the $4.3 billion in unfunded liability that Congress transfered to D.C. when the city won Home Rule in the late 1970s, the White House said.

Franklin Raines, Office of Management and Budget chief, said during a White House press briefing on the plan, that it would save the city about $770 million over five years. Raines was joined by Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin.
Raines stressed that U.S. assistance hinges on the District taking specific steps to improve its performance.

OMB's chief said the steps will be outlined in a memorandum of understanding to be hammered out by the federal and district governments and the city's congressionally appointed financial control board.
Raines said today's plan "gives the city a major opportunity to get its house in order and stop the flow of people leaving."
"(But) it's not a magic wand that will make the District's problems go away," Raines said. "DC has a lot of work to do to balance its budget a year early," he said.

The White House plan would require D.C. to balance its budget in 1998, instead of a current 1999 deadline set by Congress under 1995 legislation creating the city's control board, headed by economist Andrew Brimmer.
It is a "tough love deal," Raines said.
The White House plan would narrow Congress' oversight of the city by ending the annual U.S. appropriations cycle for D.C., the outline said.
